kept.raw0: {{c1::Germ}} cells (spermatogonia) maintain the germ pool and produce primary spermatocytes
The first stage of spermatogenesis is {{c1::DNA replication (interphase)}} of {{c2::spermatogonia}} to generate the {{c2::primary spermatocytes}}
After the primary spermatocyte has been formed, it undergoes {{c1::meiosis I}} to become a(n) {{c2::secondary spermatocyte}}
After the secondary spermatocyte has been formed, it undergoes {{c1::meiosis II}} to become a(n) {{c2::spermatid}}
After spermatids have been formed from secondary spermatocytes, they undergo {{c1::spermiogenesis}} to form {{c2::spermatozoa}}

What changes occur during the process of spermiogenesis?

- Loss of {{c1::cytoplasmic contents}}
- Gain of a(n) {{c1::acrosomal}} cap
- Development of a(n) {{c1::flagellum}}

After which stage of spermatogenesis does the diploid sperm become haploid?

{{c1::Meiosis I (primary spermatocyte to secondary spermatocyte)}}
The primary location for the maturation and storage of sperm is the {{c1::epididymis}}
In the developing ovaries, primordial germ cells produce {{c1::oogonia}} by {{c2::mitotic}} divisions until gestational weeks {{c3::20}} to {{c3::24}}
{{c1::DNA replication (interphase)::Process}} of oogonia generates the {{c2::primary oocytes}} (arrested in prophase 1)
Beginning at ovulation, primary oocytes (diploid) begin to complete {{c1::meiosis I}} to form {{c2::secondary oocytes}} (haploid)
After fertilization, the secondary oocyte completes {{c1::meiosis II}} to form a(n) {{c2::ovum}}
Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase I of meiosis I for years until {{c1::ovulation}}
Secondary oocytes are arrested in metaphase II of meiosis II until {{c1::fertilization}}
The male gonads consist of three cell types: {{c1::germ}} cells, {{c1::Sertoli}} cells, and {{c1::Leydig}} cells
The {{c2::Leydig}} cells of the male gonads synthesize {{c1::testosterone}}
{{c3::Sertoli}} cells (males) secrete {{c1::inhibin B::specific}}, which serves to inhibit {{c2::FSH}} secretion
{{c2::Sertoli}} cells secrete {{c1::androgen-binding protein}} which serves to maintain local levels of testosterone
{{c1::Tight junctions}} between adjacent {{c3::Sertoli}} cells form the {{c2::blood-testis}} barrier, which isolates gametes from autoimmune attack
{{c1::Sertoli}} cells function to support and nourish developing spermatogonia
Leydig cells secrete {{c1::testosterone}} in the presence of {{c2::LH}}
The pituitary hormone {{c1::FSH}} acts on the {{c2::Sertoli}} cells to maintain spermatogenesis
The pituitary hormone {{c1::LH}} acts on the {{c2::Leydig}} cells to promote testosterone synthesis
The functional unit of the ovaries is the single {{c1::ovarian follicle}}, which comprises one germ cell surrounded by endocrine cells
The first stage (long) of ovarian follicle development involves development of a(n) {{c1::primary}} follicle from a primordial follicle
The second stage (short) of ovarian follicle development involves the development of a(n) {{c1::Graafian}} follicle from a primary/secondary follicle
In the {{c1::granulosa}} cells of the ovary, testosterone is converted to {{c2::17β-estradiol::specific}} via the enzyme {{c3::aromatase}}
In the ovaries, aromatase activity is stimulated by the hormone {{c1::FSH}}
In the middle of the menstrual cycle, {{c1::ovulation}} occurs {{c2::14}} days prior to menses
In the middle of the menstrual cycle, estradiol {{c1::stimulates}} FSH and LH secretion
During the luteal phase of the menstrual cycle, the {{c1::corpus luteum}} begins to develop
The luteal phase of the menstrual cycle is dominated by the hormone {{c1::progesterone}}, causing increased {{c2::vascularity}} and {{c2::secretory}} activity of the endometrium
After implantation occurs, {{c2::syncytiotrophoblasts}} of the placenta begin secreting {{c1::hCG}} to maintain the corpus luteum
The function of hCG is to maintain the {{c1::corpus luteum}} by acting like LH for the first {{c2::8-10}} weeks of pregnancy
Anovulatory cycle is a menstrual cycle that lacks {{c1::ovulation}}
Anovulatory cycle results in an estrogen-driven proliferative phase, but no {{c1::progesterone}}-driven {{c1::secretory}} phase
Patients with PCOS may have {{c1::infertility}} and {{c1::irregular menses}} due to anovulation from failed {{c2::follicular maturation}}
